items.title: Agility Robotics plants its flag in Tesla’s backyard
items.summary: Johnson is currently leading Agility through a reverse-merger that is expected to make it the first pure-play humanoid robot company on the public markets later this year. Founded in 2015 by a group of researchers who developed new techniques that allow robots to safely walk on two legs, Agility is trying to capitalize on its lead over a newer generation of AI-inspired robotic startups like Figure, 1X, the Bot Company, or Sunday Robotics. [...] Unlike many of the newer entrants to the humanoid space, Agility isn’t planning to offer in-home humanoid robots anytime soon. It’s a view that jibes with that of most independent robotics experts, who believe today’s most powerful robots aren’t safe enough for consumer use. Digit operates in a human-free space right now, but the version 5, expected to be unveiled this fall, will have the ability to sense humans and won’t need to be kept in a robot-only zone. [...] While Agility doesn’t have Tesla’s capital, it does have a robot, Digit, that is already useful in the real world. The robot is already generating revenue, carrying totes and bins in manufacturing and warehouse settings for customers like Amazon, GXO, Schaeffler, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. The company says it has secured $300 million in contract orders for its robots.

items.title: Robots Are Coming — But Not Everywhere
items.summary: “The ChatGPT moment for robotics is coming,” declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 2025. Humanoid robotics will be adopted unevenly, across diverging use cases and geographies. Leaders need to reset their strategies for a more complex, jagged path to scale.

items.title: She's 27. Works a forge — hot metal, rollers, a shop that glows orange all shift.
items.summary:
She's 27. Works a forge — hot metal, rollers, a shop that glows orange all shift.

Last month: ~$4,500 in wages, ~$5,000 from filming it.

Here's the strange part. 

The most replayed moment in her videos isn't the fire or the machines. It's a one-second close-up of her face covered in soot.

Think about what that shot competes against. 

The entire feed is optimized faces — filters, ring lights, skincare routines, a billion-dollar industry devoted to looking flawless. 

And in the middle of it: a face that just did eight hours of real work. It stops people cold, because it's the one thing in the feed that isn't asking to be liked.

The dirt is the receipt. 

No caption could prove what that one second proves.

Fire does the rest. 

Humans have stared at glowing metal for thousands of years — the scroll just made it vertical. 

Her backdrop is the oldest attention magnet on earth, and she gets it free with the shift.

She films almost nothing on purpose. 

The phone stands at the edge of the station, the shift happens. 

AI picks the moments, cuts them, writes the hooks, schedules the week. 

Her editing time: zero.

At 120K followers, workwear and safety gear brands pay $1,500-3,000 per integration — gloves, boots, eyewear shown doing their actual job in real heat. 

Affiliate links on that same gear earn around the clock. 

Platform payouts stack underneath.

The shop didn't change. 

The heat didn't change. 

She just stopped washing the proof off before anyone saw it.

Every job leaves marks like that — dust, calluses, burns, paint. Most people hide them. 

On camera, they're the most convincing thing you own.

items.title: The Pentagon built a disaster zone for the most advanced robots on Earth.
items.summary:
The Pentagon built a disaster zone for the most advanced robots on Earth.

Then it asked them to open a door.

They fell over.

The 2015 DARPA Robotics Challenge was created after Fukushima exposed an uncomfortable truth: humans could build robots for war, factories and laboratories, but not one reliable enough to enter a collapsing nuclear facility for us.

So 23 teams brought their best machines to California.

The tasks sounded almost insulting:

Drive a vehicle. Get out. Open a door. Turn a valve. Cut through a wall. Walk across rubble. Climb stairs.

Things a human could do without thinking.

But the robots had no safety cables. Communications were deliberately degraded. Every machine had to negotiate gravity, friction and balance in real time.

One robot reached for a door and collapsed backward.

Another stepped from its vehicle and folded onto the concrete.

Others fell while turning, walking or simply trying to remain upright.

Some weighed nearly 400 pounds. Once they hit the ground, the run was often over.

The internet treated the footage as comedy. DARPA released an entire compilation of the falls.

But it may be the most honest robotics demo ever filmed.

Every polished video shows the one attempt where the machine and the world agreed. DARPA showed what happened when the floor was slightly different, weight shifted unexpectedly or one foot landed a few centimeters from where the software believed it was.

The robots understood the task.

They failed the contact.

Three teams eventually completed all eight challenges. That was an extraordinary achievement. But the machines falling revealed the harder problem: intelligence can choose the correct action and still lose to reality while executing it.

One engineer summarized robotics in a sentence:

“In robotics, if you don’t plan to fail, you’re going to fail. You have to just count on failure.”

A language model can regenerate a bad answer.

A 386-pound robot does not get another token.

Gravity completes the answer for it.

The next breakthrough will not be the robot that performs a task once on camera. It will be the one that notices the slip, catches itself, recovers and works again tomorrow.

AI always looks smartest before physics gets a vote.

I’m not sure how to feel about this. What are your thoughts?

This 22 year-old, third grade student teacher posted a Snapchat that got her arrested in no time! 

Incident Overview
•The Post: Written by 22-year-old student-teacher Kristen Volpe while working on a third-grade lesson plan at John L. Hensey Elementary School in Washington, Illinois.  She posted this message asking, "I was halfway through my lesson plan and one of my students pressed the power button on my computer lesson plan is gone chat do I sh00t the child or just the whole school". 
•The Context: Volpe stated the message was an exasperated joke sent via Snapchat to a private group chat with just three people (her boyfriend and two roommates) after a student turned off her computer and erased her work. 
•The Flag and Arrest: Snapchat’s automated safety/AI monitoring flagged the wording and reported it to the FBI, who then notified the Tazewell County Sheriff's Office. Deputies arrived at the school and arrested her within an hour of the message.
•The Outcome: Volpe was booked for disorderly conduct, and the charges were later dropped after she completed a deferred prosecution program.

items.title: 10 agent evals every AI engineer should know
items.summary:
10 agent evals every AI engineer should know

1) golden set

a frozen set of cases you run after every prompt model or tool change

use it as your baseline to see whether the system improved or quietly broke

OpenAI Evals helps you build repeatable benchmark sets and compare model changes

→ https://t.co/dr1GZlC75R

2) llm as judge

a second model scores open ended answers against a written rubric

use it when there is no exact output to compare against

OpenEvals provides ready made evaluators for LLM applications

→ https://t.co/S2yhnByFIP

3) rubric scoring

score correctness tone safety and cost separately

one quality number hides the problem

DeepEval helps you create custom metrics and score every dimension independently

→ https://t.co/q9Z6Xmixia

4) trajectory eval

grade the path the agent took

not only the final answer

AgentEvals checks agent actions decisions and tool calls across the full trajectory

→ https://t.co/0oziAl54az

5) tool unit tests

test every tool with fixed inputs and outputs

no model in the loop

MCP Inspector helps you inspect and test MCP servers tools and responses separately

→ https://t.co/IVmt5qpWIN

6) regression suite

replay previous runs against every new prompt model or toolset

then compare the results

Promptfoo helps you run repeatable eval suites catch regressions and add checks to CI

→ https://t.co/zxi2PuWuhe

7) a b in prod

split real traffic between two versions and compare actual outcomes

GrowthBook provides feature flags controlled experiments and product analytics

→ https://t.co/DGlE3JjDD3

8) human review

sample real runs and let a person grade them honestly

use it to calibrate your automated judge

Argilla helps teams collect human feedback review outputs and build better datasets

→ https://t.co/QHWb7skWjr

9) shadow run

let the candidate run on real traffic while its output is shown to nobody

use it before a risky rollout

Langfuse helps you trace production runs compare candidates and monitor eval results

→ https://t.co/IrhDf38tRn

10) red team

attack the system before somebody else does

jailbreaks prompt injection data leaks and tool abuse

Garak scans LLM systems for vulnerabilities and unsafe behavior

→ https://t.co/w8ObyW4ZKv

offline evals tell you it works

online evals tell you it still works

you probably do not need all ten today

start with the two that would have caught your last outage
